Your next step as a writer

From good description to a well-developed story

01

Keep your strengths

Your teacher noticed effective vocabulary, descriptive phrases and good organisation. Use these strengths to help the reader understand what matters.

02

Make the topic explicit

Show who needs help, what help is needed, and what the character actually does. Writing “I was kind” cannot do this work by itself.

03

Develop cause and effect

Let the setting affect the problem. Show a decision, specific help and a believable result. Make the final reflection grow from these events.

Your teacher’s main message: develop the setting and key details, link the story clearly to the topic, and connect the ending to the lesson learnt. Your next challenge is depth as well as accuracy.
Stage 1 · Look before you read

Your new task: A Kind Deed

Write a composition of at least 120 words about a kind deed.

The three pictures are not arranged in sequence. Base your composition on one or more of them. You may include other relevant ideas.

A · An umbrellaB · A torn schoolbagC · A bus at a bus stop
  • Who needed help, and why?
  • What made the kind deed a meaningful choice?
  • How did the person help, and what changed as a result?
  • How did the experience affect the people involved?

This is a new practice task inspired by the format of your school sheet, with original illustrations. The 698-word model is an extended learning example, not an exam word-count target. Follow your teacher’s expectations and finish within your actual time limit.

Stage 2 · Build your own version

Observe → infer → choose

A picture gives you evidence. You supply a plausible story. Separate what you can actually see from what you imagine.

What is visible?

Choose a picture. Name three concrete details. Do not invent the character’s feelings yet.

What could it mean?

Suggest two different problems or story ideas. Then choose one that fits “a kind deed”.

Picture test: If you removed your chosen picture from the story, would an important cause, action or decision disappear? A meaningful picture does more than decorate the setting.

Seven questions for a stronger plan

Your notes stay in this browser when local saving is available.

Tell your plot in one breath: “At ______, ______ needed help because ______. I chose to ______ even though ______. By the end, ______.”

Before the model: test your thinking

Is it kindness?

Would the action directly help a particular person? Have you shown compassion or understanding?

Is it developed?

Can a reader picture the helpful actions? “I helped him” is a summary. Explain how.

Is it believable?

Do the time, place and actions fit together? Does a child seek adult help when needed?

Stage 3 · Your notebook, explained

Six notes to turn into writing habits

1 · Keep speech marks next to the spoken words

Your note is about spacing. Do not leave a gap just inside the quotation marks.

Incorrect spacing: “ Please wait, ” I said.

Correct: “Please wait,” I said.

The comma sits inside the closing speech mark. There is a normal space after the closing speech mark before I said.

2 · No room on the line? Move neatly to the next line

In handwriting, do not squeeze a word into the margin or detach its closing punctuation to make it fit. If a word will not fit, begin it on the next line. Keep speech marks close to the words they belong to.

Different rule: when a different person speaks, begin a new paragraph. Simply reaching the end of a line does not create a new paragraph.

3 · “Comma before the quotation” depends on the sentence

Your note applies when a reporting clause introduces the speech:

I said, “Please wait.”

When the speech comes first, the comma goes inside the closing speech mark:

“Please wait,” I said.

A question mark or exclamation mark replaces that comma:

“Are you all right?” I asked.
“Watch out!” she shouted.

Keep she lowercase because she shouted is a speech tag. The pronoun I is always capitalised.

An action is not a speech tag. Use a full stop:

“Please wait.” I put down my bag.

Try: Add punctuation to Daniel said My bag has split.

Check your punctuation
Daniel said, “My bag has split.”
4 · Keep one narrative point of view

If the narrator is I, keep referring to that storyteller as I / me / my. Do not suddenly call the same narrator he without a clear reason.

I opened my umbrella. He decided to help.
I opened my umbrella. I decided to help.

You may still use he or she for other characters: “I helped Daniel because he was struggling.” Also, I inside another character’s dialogue refers to that speaker, not automatically to the narrator.

In first-person writing, avoid claiming to know another character’s private thoughts. Show evidence: “His shoulders relaxed” or “He told me he felt relieved.”

5 · Follow your teacher’s instruction about contractions

Your notebook says “No contractions in formal writing.” For this exercise, use full forms throughout, including dialogue: did not, could not, I would, it is.

Contractions can be natural in fictional dialogue, and they appear in the supplied school models. That does not make your notebook useless: follow the specific classroom instruction for the piece you are submitting. This new model consistently uses full forms.

Do not remove every apostrophe: the boy’s bag shows possession; it is not a contraction.

6 · Show a specific act of kindness, compassion and empathy

Empathy: understanding how another person may feel.
Compassion: caring about their difficulty and wanting to help.
The kind deed: a concrete action that helps them.

Need → understanding → choice → helpful action → effect

All five links should make sense. A story about an accident needs to develop the help if the topic is A Kind Deed. Mentioning kindness only in the final sentence is not enough.

Ask: Which actions prove the title? What difficulty does each action reduce?

Useful extra check: keep the main events in the past tense. A short earlier memory may begin with had + past participle. A general truth in the final reflection may use the present tense. Make time changes clear.
Pause before the reveal

You are the writer first.

Explain your chosen picture, the person’s need, three helpful actions and your ending. Then compare your choices with one possible model.

The model, story map and vocabulary explanations are hidden.

Stage 4 · One possible model

The Bus I Let Go

Topic: A Kind Deed · 698 words · First-person narration · A mostly chronological story with a brief memory

Read once for meaning: What does the narrator give up? What does Daniel gain? Then turn on the craft highlights to study how the writing works.
Beat 01 · Setting + personal goal

Rain rattled against the library windows as I zipped up my backpack and lifted my tote of library books. Outside, buses hissed to a stop beside the crowded shelter. I checked my watch. If I caught the next bus, I would be home in time for the football match I had been looking forward to all week. With my umbrella tucked under one arm, I hurried towards the exit.

Beat 02 · A specific need

A sharp ripping sound made me turn. Near the doorway, a younger boy stood beside a blue schoolbag. Its bottom seam had split. Exercise books, pencils and loose worksheets lay scattered across the wet pavement. One sheet slid towards a puddle. The boy lunged for it, but a gust of wind sent another skimming beyond his reach. People stepped around the mess. Nobody stopped.

Beat 03 · Empathy + hesitation

My bus appeared at the traffic lights. I tightened my grip on my umbrella. The shelter was only a short dash away. Surely the boy could pick everything up himself? Then I noticed how his fingers fumbled with the slippery pages. His lower lip trembled as he tried to gather them into a pile. I remembered dropping my art folder in the rain the previous year. The colours had run before I could save my drawing. I knew how helpless he must feel.

Beat 04 · The turning point

For a moment, I stood rooted to the spot, caught between the approaching bus and the boy at my feet. Then a worksheet landed face down in the puddle. That settled it. The match could wait.

Beat 05 · Help begins

“Let me hold this over your books,” I said, opening my umbrella. I knelt beside him and tilted it towards the scattered pages. Cold drops trickled down the back of my neck, but the books beneath the umbrella stayed dry.

The boy looked up. “My project is in there,” he said, pointing at a sodden folder. His voice was barely audible above the rain.

Beat 06 · Practical action + a small cost

I rescued the folder and placed it on top of my bag, away from the puddle. While he collected the pencils, I gathered the loose sheets and slipped them between two exercise books so that the wind could not scatter them again. “We can sort them out inside,” I told him. We carried everything back through the library doors. Behind us, the bus doors folded shut. I watched it pull away, then turned back to the boy.

Beat 07 · A believable improvement

Inside, I asked the librarian where we could put the wet things. She cleared a small table near the entrance and brought some paper towels. We blotted the covers gently and laid the damp worksheets flat. Several words had blurred, but most of the project was still readable. The boy, whose name was Daniel, let out a shaky breath. His shoulders slowly relaxed.

Beat 08 · A second need

There was still the torn bag to deal with. I took the books out of my reusable tote and packed them into my backpack. Then I offered Daniel the empty tote.

He hesitated. “But how will I give it back?”

Beat 09 · Follow-through

“We can leave it with the librarian when you return,” I suggested. She nodded, and Daniel carefully lowered his books into it. At his request, the librarian phoned his mother, who was waiting at home. While we waited for her, I helped him check that none of his worksheets were missing.

Beat 10 · Visible effects

When his mother arrived, Daniel lifted the tote to show her. “He stopped to help me,” he said. She thanked me, her worried expression softening. Daniel gave me a small smile. “You even got wet because of me.” I glanced at my damp sleeve and shrugged. A few minutes earlier, he had been struggling to stop his work from washing away. Now it was safely packed beside him.

Beat 11 · A reflection earned by the story

By the time I reached home, the match had already begun. Yet the part I had missed seemed less important than it had outside the library. As I left my umbrella open to dry, I thought about Daniel kneeling among those scattered pages. I had not stopped the rain or saved every word on his project. I had simply stopped, shared what I had and stayed until he no longer had to face the problem alone. That was what made the deed kind.

Stage 5 · Read like a writer

Why the story answers the topic

The kind deed is developed through a chain of decisions and actions. The final sentence names what the story has already demonstrated.

Opening
The rain makes the books vulnerable. The bus and football match give the narrator something to want. The umbrella and tote are introduced before they become useful.
Need
The split bag, moving worksheets and slippery pages explain why Daniel needs help. The setting creates the problem rather than simply describing the weather.
Empathy
The narrator sees trembling and fumbling, then recalls a ruined drawing. A brief memory explains why he understands Daniel; it does not take over the story.
Choice
The approaching bus makes delay feel costly. “The match could wait” signals a clear decision. A moral choice does not need a dangerous rescue.
Helpful action
Shelter the work → collect it → move it inside → dry it → replace the damaged carrying bag → contact a parent → check the pages. Each step meets a particular need.
Effect
Daniel lets out a shaky breath, relaxes and has his work safely packed. These changes are evidence of help. His mother’s thanks support the outcome; they are not the only proof.
Ending
The opening goal returns: the narrator misses part of the match. Its importance has changed. The umbrella also returns, connecting the final reflection to a real object in the story.

The pictures have jobs

Umbrella → a tool

It protects the papers and shows that the narrator is willing to get a little wet.

Torn bag → a cause

It causes the spill and creates a second problem after the pages are gathered: how to carry them home.

Bus → a choice

It makes the narrator’s hesitation visible and shows the small cost of stopping.

This model uses all three pictures because they connect naturally. A different strong story could use only one. Picture count does not replace meaningful development.
Why is the model longer? What would you trim in a timed attempt?

Its length comes mainly from causes, a decision, several helpful actions and visible consequences. It does not keep adding unrelated adventures.

If time is short, shorten the opening, reduce the memory to one sentence and combine some drying or waiting details. Protect the main chain: need → meaningful decision → concrete help → result → reflection.

For example, the waiting details could become: “The librarian called Daniel’s mother while I helped him check his worksheets.” Keep the tote solution, because otherwise the torn-bag problem remains unresolved.

This is a study model, not a promise that 700 words earn a higher mark. A shorter, complete and accurate composition can be stronger than a long, repetitive one.

A useful distinction: a brief memory versus a frame story

The school model about the lost girl pauses for a memory of being lost. That memory builds empathy. Our new model does something similar with the ruined drawing.

The school model about Auntie May uses a larger frame: an old thank-you note triggers the main memory, and Mum’s voice returns the narrator to the opening scene.

Frame scene→ clear flashback→ main event→ return to frame

A frame can give an object emotional meaning, but you must manage the time changes clearly. It is optional. Use it only if you can still develop the main incident fully.

Stage 6 · Words that do a job

Inside the new model: meaning, effect, control

Study what each expression does. Then practise using it in a fresh situation. Do not squeeze all of these phrases into one paragraph.

Rain rattled against the library windows
Sound + setting

Meaning: The rain made a quick series of tapping sounds.

Why it works here: The sound immediately places us inside the library and prepares us for the wet-paper problem.

Useful pattern: rattle against + a surface

Hail rattled against the roof of the bus shelter.

Use carefully: Use it for a repeated sharp sound, not silent mist.

buses hissed to a stop
Sound + precise movement

Meaning: The buses stopped with a hissing sound, such as air escaping from their brakes.

Why it works here: It makes the transport setting audible without a long explanation.

Useful pattern: subject + sound verb + to a stop

The train squealed to a stop beside the platform.

Use carefully: Choose a sound that matches the vehicle. Do not add sound effects to every sentence.

lay scattered across the wet pavement
Visual detail

Meaning: The things were spread untidily over the pavement.

Why it works here: We can picture the mess and understand why collecting it will take effort.

Useful pattern: things + lay scattered across + place

Broken crayons lay scattered across the classroom floor.

Use carefully: Here lay is the past tense of lie (be positioned). Laid usually needs an object: I laid the book down.

his fingers fumbled with the slippery pages
Action reveals difficulty

Meaning: His fingers tried to handle the pages awkwardly and unsuccessfully.

Why it works here: It shows the practical problem instead of simply calling him helpless.

Useful pattern: fumble with + an object

With cold fingers, I fumbled with the zip of my jacket.

Use carefully: Fumble is not the same as hold. It suggests difficulty or clumsiness.

stood rooted to the spot
Hesitation

Meaning: Stayed completely still for a moment.

Why it works here: The narrator is paused between two choices. It slows the turning point.

Useful pattern: stand / stood rooted to the spot

I stood rooted to the spot when I saw the shattered vase.

Use carefully: Use for a genuine pause. Do not have the character walking or running in the same instant.

That settled it. The match could wait.
Pace + decision

Meaning: That event ended the hesitation. The narrator decided the match was less urgent.

Why it works here: Two short sentences make the choice firm after a longer paragraph of thoughts.

Useful pattern: trigger → short decision → action

The puppy shivered again. That settled it. I called for help.

Use carefully: Make “that” refer to something clear. A decision must be followed by action.

Cold drops trickled down the back of my neck
Touch + small sacrifice

Meaning: Small drops moved slowly down the narrator’s skin.

Why it works here: The sensation shows the physical cost of sheltering someone else’s things.

Useful pattern: liquid + trickled down + surface

Sweat trickled down my forehead as I pushed the trolley.

Use carefully: Trickled suggests a small flow. A huge wave does not usually trickle.

barely audible above the rain
Sound + emotion

Meaning: So quiet that it was difficult to hear over the rain.

Why it works here: The boy’s quiet voice contrasts with the weather and suggests distress.

Useful pattern: voice / sound + was barely audible above + noise

Her reply was barely audible above the cheering.

Use carefully: Audible means able to be heard. It does not mean understandable or sensible.

so that the wind could not scatter them again
Purpose

Meaning: The narrator arranged the pages in a way that prevented another spill.

Why it works here: It explains why the action is helpful. This is development, even without fancy vocabulary.

Useful pattern: action + so that + intended result

I moved the chair aside so that she could pass.

Use carefully: Use a result that the action could reasonably achieve.

blotted the covers gently
Precise helpful action

Meaning: Pressed absorbent material against the covers to take up moisture.

Why it works here: Blotted is more precise than cleaned. Gently suits fragile, wet material.

Useful pattern: blot + wet surface + with + absorbent material

She blotted the spill with a paper towel.

Use carefully: Blotting is pressing, not rubbing hard. Choose the verb that matches the real action.

let out a shaky breath
Body language

Meaning: Breathed out unsteadily after tension or worry.

Why it works here: It begins the change from panic to relief without claiming to know every thought.

Useful pattern: let out + a breath / sigh / gasp

When I found my passport, I let out a long breath.

Use carefully: A shaky breath can signal several emotions. Let the situation make the meaning clear.

her worried expression softening
A visible emotional change

Meaning: Her face looked less tense or worried.

Why it works here: It shows the mother’s response as she sees the problem has been handled.

Useful pattern: expression / voice + softened

His expression softened when he heard the apology.

Use carefully: Keep the person clear. Do not write “the bag’s expression softened”.

stayed until he no longer had to face the problem alone
Reflection + theme

Meaning: Continued helping until the person had support.

Why it works here: The ending defines kindness through the exact behaviour in this story.

Useful pattern: stayed / helped until + meaningful change

I stayed until my partner felt ready to try again.

Use carefully: Avoid copying this ending into an unrelated story. Match the reflection to the events.

Two sentence structures worth borrowing

“While…”: connect actions happening at the same time
While he collected the pencils, I gathered the loose sheets.

Job: makes cooperation visible and avoids a string of sentences beginning with Then I….

Build it: While + subject + past-tense verb, subject + past-tense verb.

Your turn: Write a sentence in which two people share a helpful task.

A participle phrase: add action without a dangling subject
I said, opening my umbrella.
Opening my umbrella, I stepped towards him.

The same person performs both actions: I speak or step, and I open the umbrella.

Opening my umbrella, the books stayed dry.

That version wrongly makes the books seem to open the umbrella. Keep the doer clear.

Your turn: Begin a sentence with Gripping the handles, …. Name the person who is gripping them immediately after the comma.

Stage 7 · Learn from your supplied school models

Good phrases are choices, not decorations

These short expressions come from the two model compositions in your photos. Notice the situation in which each one works before adapting it.

“a bustling Saturday afternoon”
Lost-child model

Meaning and job: Bustling means busy and full of activity. It efficiently establishes the crowded mall.

Fresh example: The market was bustling with shoppers.

Use carefully: Do not use bustling for an almost empty corridor.

“tears glistened in her frightened eyes”
Lost-child model

Meaning and job: Glistened means shone with reflected light. It makes the tears visible; the surrounding actions establish fear.

Fresh example: Raindrops glistened on the leaves.

Use carefully: Glisten describes light, not sadness by itself.

“For a moment, I was torn.”
Lost-child model

Meaning and job: Torn means unable to decide between competing choices. Here the narrator wants the sale but also wants to help.

Fresh example: I was torn between joining the game and helping my brother.

Use carefully: Name or establish the two choices. It does not simply mean worried.

“Seconds crawled by.”
Lost-child model

Meaning and job: Time seems to pass painfully slowly while they wait. This is personification: seconds do not literally crawl.

Fresh example: Minutes crawled by as we waited for news.

Use carefully: Use it at an anxious wait, not during a fast chase. One well-placed image is enough.

“crouched down so that we were at eye level”
Lost-child model

Meaning and job: The action reduces the physical distance between the narrator and the small child. It makes reassurance concrete.

Fresh example: I crouched beside the child so that she could see my face.

Use carefully: Its power comes from empathy and purpose, not from a difficult word.

“My mind was in a whirl.”
Auntie May model

Meaning and job: Thoughts felt confused and rushed as the narrator considered conflicting demands.

Fresh example: My mind was in a whirl as I tried to decide what to do.

Use carefully: Follow it with the actual thoughts or choices; the phrase alone does not develop a dilemma.

“beads of perspiration”
Auntie May model

Meaning and job: Small drops of sweat. In the model, they show the cleaner’s effort and later the narrator’s effort.

Fresh example: Beads of perspiration dotted his forehead.

Use carefully: Perspiration is a formal word for sweat. It is useful only when heat or effort makes sense.

“with all my might”
Auntie May model

Meaning and job: Using all one’s strength. It suits the effort of pushing a heavy trolley.

Fresh example: I pushed against the heavy door with all my might.

Use carefully: It is excessive for lifting a pencil or turning a page.

“snapped me back to reality”
Auntie May model

Meaning and job: Abruptly brought the narrator out of a memory and back to the surrounding scene. It closes the flashback frame.

Fresh example: The school bell snapped me back to reality.

Use carefully: Use it only when someone has been absorbed in thoughts, a memory or a daydream.

“a reminder of the day I chose kindness”
Auntie May model

Meaning and job: The thank-you note carries the meaning of the whole experience. The object links the opening, main event and ending.

Fresh example: The dented medal became a reminder of the day I refused to give up.

Use carefully: Build that connection earlier. An object introduced only in the last sentence may feel forced.

Grammar detective: one sentence in the supplied lost-child model begins “Watching them together, warmth spread through my chest.” The intended meaning is clear, but the opening phrase technically makes warmth the watcher. A cleaner version is: “As I watched them together, I felt warmth spread through my chest.” Even model compositions are worth reading critically.
Stage 8 · Transfer the skill

Try first. Open the explanation afterwards.

1 · Develop the help

Improve this: “I helped the boy. He was happy.”

Add two practical actions, explain the purpose of one, and show one visible change in the boy.

Reveal one possible answer
I slid the loose worksheets between two exercise books so that the wind could not scatter them. Then I held the umbrella over his bag while he packed. His hands stopped trembling, and he gave me a small smile.

The verbs explain the help; so that explains its purpose; the final actions suggest relief. Your answer can use different actions if they fit your story.

2 · Choose the phrase that fits

A character is waiting anxiously for a parent to arrive. Which is more suitable: “Seconds crawled by” or “with all my might”? Explain why.

Reveal the explanation

“Seconds crawled by” fits the slow-feeling, anxious wait. With all my might describes physical effort. A good phrase must match what is happening.

3 · Repair speech, viewpoint and contraction

I told Daniel “ Don’t worry ”. He opened his umbrella to help.

The storyteller is I, and the storyteller opens the umbrella. Correct the passage using your notebook rules.

Reveal one correction
I told Daniel, “Do not worry.” I opened my umbrella to help.

There is a comma before the speech, no extra space inside the speech marks, a full stop inside the closing mark, a full form instead of a contraction, and a consistent first-person narrator.

4 · Write an ending that belongs to your story

Return to an object or choice from your own plan. Explain what it now means to the narrator, using one or two sentences.

Check the job your ending does

Does it follow from your actual events? Does it show a changed understanding? Can you point to an earlier detail it connects with? A lesson should clarify the experience, not introduce a different topic.

Before you submit

My personal checking routine

Check content first, then language. Your teacher’s comments make both steps important.

About this workshop. All teaching text is in English. It is tailored to the supplied P4 task sheet, the handwritten “Composition mistakes” notes, the teacher’s writing-feedback sheet and the two supplied “A Kind Deed” models. The original student composition was not supplied, so this lesson responds to the feedback rather than diagnosing unseen sentences.

The task, illustrations and new model are original learning materials. No school endorsement or score prediction is implied. The report does not reproduce the child’s name, class, marks or document photographs.

Illustration credits and prompt

Generated using the built-in image-generation tool. Prompt: one landscape sheet with three independent, equally sized picture panels; an open dark-blue umbrella, a torn schoolbag with exercise books and loose worksheets on a pavement, and a Singapore-style public bus at a bus stop. Clear line drawing with light watercolour, white gutters, no wording, numerals or logos, and no helping action or story resolution.
